title: Compatibility Matters: A Framework for Token-Level Teacher Selection in On-Policy Distillation

paper.title: Compatibility Matters: A Framework for Token-Level Teacher Selection in On-Policy Distillation
paper.abstract: Abstract On-policy distillation (OPD) has recently been introduced as a promising paradigm for continual learning, where a student policy can be supervised at the token-level. Typically, OPD is performed using a single teacher per prompt rollout (or even per training run). However, this ignores a whole other axis of flexibility that is available due to the on-policy nature — token-level teacher selection during rollouts. Building on this insight, we theoretically explore what makes a teacher and a student compatible for OPD, and leverage our findings to derive several empirical heuristics for teacher selection. In particular, our framework captures several desiderata for OPD: compatible teacher-student reasoning patterns, teacher competence, and induced student diversity. Theoretically, we categorize several types of teacher routing schemes, and we prove that under different scenarios, different routing schemes are likely to be beneficial for optimization and student diversity. We back up our findings with extensive experimental results in domains such as math, coding, kernel generation, and visual reasoning, where we find upwards of 10 percentage points of improvement on pass@ k k when compared to vanilla OPD and the teacher experts on certain tasks, indicating both capability improvement and diversity over high-quality responses.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Modern LLM training generally follows the framework of a large-scale pretraining phase on corpora from the real world ( Brown et al., 2020 ; Olmo et al., 2026 ) , such as internet and human-curated data, followed by a post-training phase, in which a base pretrained LLM is fine-tuned to elicit domain-specific gains in capability, most notably in domains such as mathematical reasoning ( Shao et al., 2024 ) , instruction following ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ) , and software engineering ( Wei et al., 2025 ) . In particular, reinforcement learning (RL) ( Christiano et al., 2023 ; DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025 ) has recently emerged as a popular paradigm for improving LLM capabilities during post-training. This approach has been well-demonstrated to bring about scalable gains over the initial pre-training phase of LLMs, and has been widely adopted amongst both open- and closed-source models. On-policy distillation ( Hinton et al., 2015 ; Agarwal et al., 2024 ) has been proposed as a promising alternative. The difference, however, is that the teacher provides dense, token-level feedback to the student rather than in RL where the single reward scalar signal guides the gradient updates. Recently, specialized versions of OPD such as on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) as well as other variants have been proposed ( Zhao et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026c ) . Separately, there have also been works inspired from classical RL literature which train a separate critic model to give an estimate of the process reward ( Bai et al., 2022 ; Venkatraman et al., 2026 ) . In this paper, we aim to give a rigorous characterization of what makes a teacher and student compatible for OPD-style training. Informally speaking, the student and teacher should not have too much distributional mismatch ( Fu et al., 2026a ; Li et al., 2026b ) ; otherwise, as we prove, the optimization landscape will be very unfavorable. Moreover, the teacher should be somewhat competent, which we will quantify later. Finally, the teacher’s supervision should induce good diversity over good responses for the student. We formalize all of these concepts in a unified manner in Section 4 . Importantly, we make an additional observation that is unique to the on-policy setting: not only can we do teacher selection for a given prompt (i.e. as in MOPD ( Ma et al., 2026 ) where prompts of a given domain are routed to the corresponding domain expert), we can actually also do teacher selection token-wise during a student rollout. The intuition for this is that different teachers may be more suitable for different parts of a student rollout (for instance, in algorithmic coding it may be useful to have a math teacher guide the mathematical reasoning prior to implementation). Overall, we summarize our contributions as follows. • First, we give a theoretical framework to ground the analysis of token-level teacher selection, in which we can decouple the contribution of teacher competence and of the teacher-student gap. • Then, within this framework, we give a unified mathematical interpretation of the confidence-based routing scheme from Yin et al. (2026) and a newly proposed representation-based routing scheme. In particular, we show in different scenarios one or the other could prove more useful as a routing scheme. Importantly, we also prove that the representation-based routing has the potential to yield more diverse student generations. • We back up our theoretical insights with experiments across many domains, including code, Triton kernel generation, math, and visual reasoning. These demonstrate the clear potential of token-level teacher selection over vanilla OPD via improvements across pass@ k k , indicating student learning of high quality and diverse responses. More importantly, we are able to have principled predictions of when a family of routing schemes is likely to be effective in practical setups. We discuss related work in Appendix A .

sections.text: Figure 1 : Triton-only entropy routing ( τ = 0.1 \tau=0.1 ; iteration 300). Here, we plot the score gap of the kernel teacher minus the thinking teacher. The full trace is included in Section H.3 , where we can observe that the blue (positive) regions on this plot correspond roughly to parts of the student rollout where Triton code is being generated, and the red parts correspond to general reasoning or thinking behavior to plan the kernel code. We study token-level teacher selection in settings that encompass the domains of math, coding, Triton kernel generation, and visual reasoning 7 7 7 Results on visual reasoning are deferred to Appendix H . . More specifically, we consider the following setups: • A synthetic math-triton task with access to respective math and Triton teachers where there is a clear way to perform teacher selection via section routing ( Section 5.1 ) • A Triton-only task with access to a thinking model and a domain expert ( Section 5.2 ) • Algorithmic coding tasks under a math and code teacher ( Section 5.3 ) Precise scoring functions used are defined in Section E.2 , as they may differ in implementation from our theoretical formulations in Section 4 . One concrete example of this is when we choose to use the Hellinger score instead of the feature distance score in some cases, due to the teacher and student having different architectures. Additional training details and evaluation protocols are given in Appendices F and G . Notably, for our score-based routing frameworks, we will generally sweep through several temperatures τ \tau , as well as choices of policy gradient implementation (i.e. either sampled token advantage or the Top-K KL). For sampled token advantage, we use τ = 0 \tau=0 (i.e. hard routing) by default. In our tables, besides reporting results on token-level routing, we also report baselines of vanilla OPD (which uses sampled token advantage by default), as well as the teachers and initial student performance.

sections.heading: 5.1 A Synthetic Math-Triton Task
sections.text: We construct more than 8000 training prompts by pairing DeepMath problems ( He et al., 2025 ) with KernelBook tasks ( Paliskara and Saroufim, 2025 ) . Each prompt requests both solutions, with the task order assigned randomly and held fixed. The student model we use is a Qwen3-4B ( Qwen Team, 2025a ) , using the non-base variant with thinking mode off. For the teachers, we use a Qwen3-4B that has gone through math RL training on DeepMath, as well as the Dr.Kernel-8B ( Liu et al., 2026a ) . We train the student for 300 updates on these composite prompts. For evaluation, we use the size 3000 set of AIME 2025 × \times KernelBench Level 2 ( OpenCompass Contributors, 2025 ; Ouyang et al., 2025 ) combinations (30 AIME problems and 100 KernelBench Level 2 problems). Joint success requires a correct math answer and a correct kernel in the same response, with kernel correctness measured by fast 0 , which gives a binary reward purely depending on correctness, without regard to speedup. Our results are shown in Table 1 , in which we compare against the baselines of the initial student model, the teachers, and vanilla OPD. sections.heading: 5.4 Interpreting Effective Routing Schemes
sections.text: We note that in the above three settings, Hellinger- or feature-based routing performed better on the code-only task and the synthetic Triton-math task, whereas the entropy-based routing performed better on the Triton-thinking task. Looking back at Equation 4 , we observe that when the LLM heads have similar magnitudes, the feature alignment ρ \rho is the useful router. Under the code-only and Triton-math task, we have access to teachers which are essentially fine-tuned versions of the base model. Empirically speaking, fine-tuning should not change head norms ‖ ω ‖ 2 \|\omega\|_{2} by much, and as such the feature alignment becomes the important term. Analogously, Equation 4 demonstrates that when the teacher features are equally (mis-)aligned with the student features, entropy becomes the useful router. Indeed, in the Triton-thinking task, neither teacher is from the same model family as the base model, so the student and the teachers naturally do not have much feature alignment. In that sense, we would expect the entropy-based routing to be more effective, which it indeed is.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: In this work, we explore token-level teacher routing as an additional axis for OPD training. To that end, we propose a theoretical framework in the log-linear setting to unify existing classes of teacher selection methods (e.g. entropy-based) as well as a new class of representation-based routing that we propose. Together, these allow us to predict empirically when one scheme may be more beneficial than the other, in the context of the trained student’s ability and output diversity. We believe there is room for much more design and improvement on this axis, as well as understanding of its downstream benefits. For instance, an interesting open question would be to understand if the diversity improvements of our teacher selection scheme can be used to create a better warm start for RL post-OPD. In addition, it would also be worthwhile to derive teacher selection metrics that are more reward-aware, beyond simply choosing the strongest teacher.

sections.heading: LLM post-training.
sections.text: Post-training LLMs with RL has generally concerned optimizing for some reward, such as a learned preference reward in RLHF [ Christiano et al., 2023 , Ouyang et al., 2022 ] or a verifiable one in RLVR [ DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025 ] . Beyond recent algorithmic innovations to the classic policy gradient algorithms [ Williams, 1992 , Sutton et al., 1999 ] such as TRPO and PPO [ Schulman et al., 2015 , Schulman et al., 2017 ] , a growing line of theoretical work has been aimed towards understanding what sorts of reward models yield favorable optimization guarantees [ Razin et al., 2025 , Shang et al., 2026 ] . In addition, there has also been an extensive line of work understanding the interplay between on- and off-policy data in training, most notably in contrasting the post-training phases of SFT and RL [ Shenfeld et al., 2025 , Wei and Kim, 2026 , Park et al., 2025 , Matsutani et al., 2026 , Huang et al., 2026 ] .

sections.heading: On-policy distillation.
sections.text: On-policy distillation (OPD) replaces the scalar reward in RL with dense token-level supervision from a teacher queried on the student’s own rollouts [ Hinton et al., 2015 , Agarwal et al., 2024 ] . G-OPD connects vanilla OPD to KL-regularized RL and separates the reward scale from the regularization strength [ Yang et al., 2026a ] , and recent work by Li et al. [2026a] finds that OPD followed by RL outperforms RL alone. A related line of work in the direction of OPD is on-policy self-distillation (OPSD), which removes the separate teacher by conditioning the same model on privileged context such as a reference solution [ Zhao et al., 2026 ] , with unsupervised [ Li et al., 2026c ] and shortcut-purified [ Shen et al., 2026 ] variants. In addition, MOPD is a way to distill from several independently trained domain experts [ Ma et al., 2026 ] .

sections.heading: OPD dynamics and prefix drift.
sections.text: Several recent works examine why dense teacher feedback can nonetheless be hard to learn from. For instance, Fu et al. [2026a] separate the token-local update from the sequence-level reverse KL gradient and identify imbalanced sampled-token signals and support mismatch as failure modes; Li et al. [2026b] find that compatible thinking patterns and genuinely new capabilities are distinct conditions for transfer; and Fu et al. [2026b] show that a single query already induces broad state visitation while the supervision itself is incorporated slowly. On the theory side, Zhang et al. [2026] show that the advantage of online over offline imitation in post-training hinges on non-realizability of the expert rather than on horizon-driven error accumulation, and Sriraman et al. [2026] show that with noisy expert feedback, OPD attains polynomial rather than exponential-in-horizon sample complexity. Additional analyses have suggested that prefixes are generally off-policy for the teacher: early-token supervision is more effective than late-token supervision [ Xie et al., 2026 ] , teacher confidence decays along student rollouts [ Liu et al., 2026b ] , and student–teacher mismatch invites length-dependent exploitation of the objective [ Wang et al., 2026 ] . Our work provides an additional theoretical perspective for understanding teachers that yield good optimization guarantees under OPD.

sections.heading: Teacher selection, student compatibility, and token-level supervision.
sections.text: A more general line of work that spans the knowledge distillation literature is understanding teacher suitability for the student. For example GRACE scores teachers by the distribution of student gradients on their outputs [ Panigrahi et al., 2025 ] , and the Rank–Surprisal Ratio proposed by Yang et al. [2026b] balances alignment with the student against informativeness. Indeed, both of these above works choose a teacher once for the entire training duration. H-OPD [ Yin et al., 2026 ] suggests the use of confidence as a way to do token-level routing, but their analysis is limited to the setting of vision tasks. Some more recent works analyze the other end of the spectrum, which is to see how little supervision one can get away with in OPD while preserving its advantages. For instance, OPSA replaces the teacher advantage on low-probability tokens [ Ding and Zhang, 2026 ] , and Liu et al. [2026c] supervise only one or two tokens per rollout. Our insight then, is that if we specialize to the on-policy training case, then we can naturally extend teacher arbitration to the token level, using different routing schemes depending on the setting.

sections.heading: Interventions for better coverage.
sections.text: The coverage principle of Chen et al. [2025] argues that the probability a model already assigns to high-quality responses governs what post-training and test-time selection can achieve. This framework has guided several follow-up works in terms of better interventions for improving coverage. For instance, TailSFT filters already-fit sequences out of SFT so that learning concentrates on under-modeled regions, improving pass@ k k before RL [ Malladi et al., 2026 ] . In addition, Cheng et al. [2026] trace the gap between pass@1 gains and pass@ N N losses after RL to a reshaping of strategy selection and connect it to coverage and transfer. The OPD-then-RL setup of Li et al. [2026a] can also be interpreted as first broadening the set of teacher-supported solutions and then concentrating probability on the successful ones. Moreover, Tuyls et al. [2026] also designs a representation-aware RL post-training scheme in order to induce better diversity of output responses. In our work, we prove that our representation-based teacher selection scheme in Section 4.3 is coverage-aware in a similar spirit; that is, our diversity analysis in Section 4.5 upper bounds the undercoverage quantity of high-quality continuations.

sections.heading: Appendix B Proofs of the Feature-Matching Teacher Selection
sections.text: We briefly describe the organization of this section below. First, in Section B.1 , we describe how teacher competence (as measured in expected reward) and teacher-student compatibility complement each other in terms of the training outcome of OPD, via the performance difference lemma; notably, this also allows us to realize the potential of token-level teacher selection over using only a single teacher. Then, in Section B.2 , we list out the properties of the gradient and optimization landscape at initialization to work towards a proof of Theorem 1 . Afterwards, in Section B.3 , we explicitly quantify the benefit of using our feature-matching selection scheme to give the full proof of Theorem 1 . Finally in Section B.4 , we provide the full proofs on how our selection scheme can improve the coverage of good response modes.

sections.heading: Separating imitation from reward.
sections.text: The gradient comparison concerns how strongly a teacher moves the student toward minimizing its KL objective with a given teacher. In the performance-difference decomposition of Section B.1 , this concerns imitation; the teacher’s competence remains in its separate reward-gap term. In general, it is an open question to quantify the trade-off between teacher competence and optimization pressures, but we would nonetheless like to include a brief discussion of success cases and failure modes of our two families of teacher selection. To kick this discussion off, we remark that in most OPD settings, the teachers have some level of competence, and this is simply due to the fact that OPD in the recent literature generally distills from a model that was either 1) a post-trained version of the student, whether via RL or the likes, 2) a bigger (and hence more capable) model from the same model family as the student, or 3) both of the above. We will operate under this mental model for the rest of our exposition in this section.

sections.heading: On the confidence-based selection scheme.
sections.text: One obvious failure mode of this selection scheme is choosing a teacher that is confidently wrong. This may happen if, for instance the teacher was post-trained on bad data that perhaps caused model collapse. However, even barring this pathological case, another failure mode is simply the decrease in diversity of student responses due to imitation of a low-entropy distribution. This is a setting that we noticed in our experiments too by checking pass@ k k , in the sense that there were cases where although the entropy-routed model had better pass@1, it was worse on pass@ k k . On the other hand, if the teacher is confidently right, then the teacher could potentially be a promising candidate for supervision. Nevertheless, if the thinking patterns do not match with the student, supervision can still remain difficult. The ideal case is where the teacher is confidently right, and the thinking patterns are compatible. In the context of our theory, this would correspond to ψ = ϕ \psi=\phi , with very large teacher head.

sections.heading: On the representation-based selection scheme.
sections.text: As with the entropy-based selection scheme, one failure mode is where the teacher (assumed to be post-trained version of the student or a variant) has been tilted towards some undesirable reward distribution. In this case, the student has no choice but to follow the teacher. Indeed, this is the big open problem in post-training, of how to calibrate competence vs. magnitude learning signal.

sections.text: In this section, we give the precise score functions S i ​ ( s t , θ j ) S_{i}(s_{t};\theta_{j}) that enter the router in Equation 2 , organized into the same three families as Section 3 , followed by the temperatures we use. In every case, the score is computed from the same prefix s t = ( x , y < t ) s_{t}=(x,y_{<t}) whose next token y t y_{t} the loss supervises, so there is no lookahead into y t y_{t} , and the resulting weights w i ​ ( s t ) w_{i}(s_{t}) are detached and held fixed during the update. Given the weights, the teacher target is the selected teacher under hard routing ( τ = 0 \tau=0 ) or the arithmetic mixture π T , w \pi_{T,w} under soft routing, which then enters either the sampled-token advantage or the top- K K KL objective exactly as described in Section E.1 .

sections.heading: Direct section routing.
sections.text: We use this in the two settings where the response has an explicit section structure. In the synthetic math–Triton task of Section 5.1 , the composite prompt asks for both solutions in a specified order and asks that each be wrapped in its own tag ( <math_solution> and <triton_solution> ). Routing is then deterministic given the tags completed so far in the prefix: before any tag is opened, we route to the teacher of the task requested first; inside an opened tag, we route to that domain’s teacher, and once a tag is closed, we route to the teacher of the remaining task. Tags appearing inside fenced or inline code are ignored, and a token that completes a tag is still routed according to the state before it. In the Triton-only task of Section 5.2 , the sections are the student’s thinking block and the answer that follows it: every token generated while the thinking block is open is routed to the thinking teacher, and every token after the closing thinking tag is routed to Dr.Kernel, again with the closing tag itself routed according to the state before it. In the notation of Equation 2 , this is equivalent to taking τ = 0 \tau=0 with S i ​ ( s t , θ j ) = 1 S_{i}(s_{t};\theta_{j})=1 for the assigned teacher and 0 0 otherwise.

sections.heading: Routing temperatures.
sections.text: Soft weights are obtained by plugging the raw scores above into Equation 2 . For entropy and feature matching, we sweep τ ∈ { 0.1 , 0.25 , 0.5 , 1 } \tau\in\{0.1,0.25,0.5,1\} , and for Hellinger routing, we sweep τ ∈ { 10 − 4 , 10 − 3 , 10 − 2 } \tau\in\{10^{-4},10^{-3},10^{-2}\} , since Hellinger distances lie in [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] and the gaps between two teachers are typically small. In each setting, we report the temperature with the best pass@1.

sections.heading: Algorithmic coding.
sections.text: The distillation prompts are the 25,276 Eurus-2-RL code training prompts [ Cui et al., 2025 ] , with 1,024 code prompts held out for validation. These are the same prompts on which the code RL expert was trained. The math RL expert is trained on DeepMath [ He et al., 2025 ] for 500 iterations, following the domain-specialization setup of Yang et al. [2026a] .

sections.heading: Synthetic math–Triton task.
sections.text: The Triton side starts from 11,621 KernelBook programs [ Paliskara and Saroufim, 2025 ] , which deduplicate by exact source code to 8,884 distinct programs. Before any length filtering, 512 programs are reserved for validation and 256 for a future test split; every remaining program is paired with a distinct, shuffled DeepMath training problem, and the math problems used for validation are excluded from math training. Composite prompts longer than 4,096 tokens are dropped, leaving 8,077 training pairs and 509 validation pairs.

sections.heading: Visual reasoning.
sections.text: The visual reasoning runs use the training set released with H-OPD [ Yin et al., 2026 ] : 54,840 image-based problems with verifiable answers drawn from MMFineReason-123K and filtered by the authors with a GPT-4.1-mini judge. Each problem comes with a Qwen3-VL-generated description of its image; the vision-language teacher receives the image, while the text-only teacher receives the question with the description appended in place of the image. The student is Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct and the teachers are Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct and the text-only Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 [ Qwen Team, 2025b , Qwen Team, 2025a ] .

sections.heading: Optimization and sampling.
sections.text: All four settings share the same recipe. The student is trained for 300 updates (400 for visual reasoning) with a batch of 128 prompts and a single rollout per prompt, sampled at temperature 1 1 and top- p = 1 p=1 with no top- k k restriction. We use AdamW with a constant learning rate of 10 − 6 10^{-6} , no warmup, and gradient clipping at 1 1 . The prompt and response token caps are 2,048 and 8,192 for algorithmic coding, 4,096 and 16,384 for the synthetic math–Triton and Triton-only tasks, and 16,384 for both in visual reasoning. Thinking mode is disabled everywhere except in the Triton-only task.

sections.text: For every evaluation task, we draw n n independent responses at temperature 1 1 and top- p = 1 p=1 with no top- k k restriction, using seeds shared across all compared models, and count the number c i c_{i} of responses that are correct for task i i . With N N tasks, we report the unbiased estimator of Chen et al. [2021] , pass ​ @ ⁡ k ^ = 1 N ​ ∑ i = 1 N [ 1 − ( n − c i k ) ( n k ) ] , \widehat{\operatorname{pass@}k}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left[1-\frac{\binom{n-c_{i}}{k}}{\binom{n}{k}}\right], (43) so that every k k for a given model is computed from the same pool of n n samples. We report pass@1 and pass@16 for the synthetic math–Triton and Triton-only tasks, pass@1 and pass@64 for algorithmic coding, and pass@1 only for visual reasoning.

sections.heading: Synthetic math–Triton.
sections.text: The evaluation set pairs the 30 AIME 2025 problems released by OpenCompass [ OpenCompass Contributors, 2025 ] with the 100 KernelBench Level 2 tasks [ Ouyang et al., 2025 ] , giving 3,000 composite prompts, each with a fixed and balanced requested order of the two parts. We evaluate on the 3,000 pairs with n = 16 n=16 responses per pair, a 16,384-token response cap, and thinking disabled. Let M ⁡ ( r ) M(r) indicate that response r r gives the correct math answer and C ⁡ ( r ) C(r) that its kernel passes all configured correctness trials (the fast 0 criterion of KernelBench). The joint score is J 0 ​ ( r ) = M ⁡ ( r ) ​ C ​ ( r ) J_{0}(r)=M(r)\,C(r) , so joint fast 0 requires both parts to be correct in the same response; the math-portion and kernel-portion columns of Table 1 report M M and C C separately.

sections.heading: Triton-only.
sections.text: We evaluate on the same 100 KernelBench Level 2 tasks with the same kernel prompt, drawing n = 16 n=16 responses per task with a 32,768-token response cap so that the thinking-mode student can complete its reasoning. Correctness is fast 0 as above, and Table 2 reports pass@1 and pass@16.

sections.heading: Algorithmic coding.
sections.text: We evaluate on the 164 HumanEval+ and 378 MBPP+ problems of EvalPlus [ Chen et al., 2021 , Austin et al., 2021 , Liu et al., 2023 ] , drawing n = 128 n=128 responses per problem. Table 3 reports pass@1 and pass@64 from this pool.

sections.heading: Visual reasoning.
sections.text: We report pass@1 only, on WeMath [ Qiao et al., 2024 ] , MathVista-mini [ Lu et al., 2024 ] , and the reasoning questions of the CharXiv validation split [ Wang et al., 2024 ] . WeMath is scored as question-level accuracy averaged over 16 sampled responses per question; MathVista-mini and CharXiv use a single sampled response per question. Final answers are extracted and graded with an LLM judge following the VLMEvalKit protocol used by H-OPD [ Yin et al., 2026 ] ; we use GPT-5.6 as the judge in place of GPT-4o-mini from the original paper.

Prompt user Find the largest rectangular area possible in a given histogram where the largest rectangle can be made of a number of contiguous bars. For simplicity, assume that all bars have the same width and the width is 1 unit, there will be N bars height of each bar will be given by the array arr. Example 1: Input: N = 7 arr[] = {6,2,5,4,5,1,6} Output: 12 Explanation: In this example the largest area would be 12 of height 4 and width 3. We can achieve this area by choosing 3rd, 4th and 5th bars. Example 2: Input: N = 8 arr[] = {7 2 8 9 1 3 6 5} Output: 16 Explanation: Maximum size of the histogram will be 8 and there will be 2 consecutive histogram. And hence the area of the histogram will be 8x2 = 16. Your Task: The task is to complete the function getMaxArea() which takes the array arr[] and its size N as inputs and finds the largest rectangular area possible and returns the answer. Expected Time Complxity : O(N) Expected Auxilliary Space : O(N) Constraints: 1 <U+2264> N <U+2264> 10ˆ{6} 0 <U+2264> arr[i] <U+2264> 10ˆ{12} Write Python code to solve the problem. Present the code in ‘‘‘python Your code ‘‘‘ at the end. You need to think first then write the Python code. assistant <think> </think> Student response To solve the largest rectangular area in a histogram problem efficiently in **O(N)** time and **O(N)** space, we can use a **monotonic stack** approach. ### Intuition: For each bar, we want to find: - The first bar to the left that is **shorter** than the current bar (left bound) - The first bar to the right that is **shorter** than the current bar (right bound) Then, the maximum area for that bar is ‘height * (right_bound - left_bound - 1)‘. This is because: - The bar can extend from ‘left_bound + 1‘ to ‘right_bound - 1‘. - The width is ‘(right_bound - left_bound - 1)‘, and the height is the height of the current bar. ### Steps: 1. Initialize an empty stack. 2. Iterate through the array: - While the stack is not empty and the current bar’s height is less than the height of the bar at the top of the stack: - Pop the top of the stack and calculate the area. - The popped bar’s height is the height of the rectangle. - The width is determined by the current index and the new top of the stack (or 0 if stack is empty). - Push the current index into the stack. 3. After the iteration, process any remaining elements in the stack in a similar way. ### Edge Cases: - If all bars are increasing, the stack will be processed at the end. - If all bars are decreasing, we process each bar as we go. ### Python Code: ‘‘‘python def getMaxArea(arr): stack = [] max_area = 0 n = len(arr) for i in range(n): while stack and arr[i] < arr[stack[-1]]: height = arr[stack.pop()] width = i if not stack else i - stack[-1] - 1 max_area = max(max_area, height * width) stack.append(i) # Process remaining bars in the stack while stack: height = arr[stack.pop()] width = n if not stack else n - stack[-1] - 1 max_area = max(max_area, height * width) return max_area ‘‘‘ ### Example Test Cases: ‘‘‘python # Example 1 print(getMaxArea([6, 2, 5, 4, 5, 1, 6])) # Output: 12 # Example 2 print(getMaxArea([7, 2, 8, 9, 1, 3, 6, 5])) # Output: 16 ‘‘‘ ### Complexity: - **Time Complexity:** O(N), as each bar is pushed and popped from the stack exactly once. - **Space Complexity:** O(N), for the stack. This solution is efficient and meets the constraints given.
